beats.intro: Chapter nine. [[sub]]Before valuing a company, an analyst must understand it. This chapter covers how to analyze a business, its revenue, its costs, and its capital.
beats.report: A company research report follows a standard shape. [[rec]]It leads with a recommendation, and target prices. [[desc]]Then the business model and strategy. [[comp]]The company's competitive position within its industry. [[fin]]The financial analysis: past results, current position, and forecasts. [[val]]A valuation, which turns the forecasts into a price. [[risk]]The risks that could make the analysis wrong. And increasingly, environmental, social and governance factors. [[note]]An initial report covers all of this in depth. Later reports update the forecasts and the recommendation.
beats.model: The first step is the business model. [[cust]]Who are the customers, and which groups matter most? [[chan]]How does the company reach them, through which sales channels? [[price]]How much does it charge, and how does it earn revenue? [[res]]Which resources, suppliers and partners deliver the product? [[src]]Good sources include regulatory filings, investor presentations and events, company visits and websites, and then industry data and other analysts.
beats.revenue: Revenue can be analyzed two ways. [[bu]]Bottom-up: build revenue from drivers, such as volume times price, product by product. A hundred units at eight euros is eight hundred. [[td]]Top-down: start with the market. If the market is eight thousand and the company has a ten percent share, revenue is eight hundred. [[grow]]Now the market grows five percent, to eighty four hundred, and the share rises to eleven percent. Revenue becomes nine twenty four, up fifteen and a half percent. [[note]]Growth can come from the market, from share, from price, or from volume. Know which.
beats.pricing: Raising prices only helps if volume holds up. That is pricing power. [[base]]Start with revenue of one hundred. [[strong]]A company with strong pricing power raises price five percent, and loses only one percent of volume. Revenue rises to about one oh four. [[weak]]A company with weak pricing power loses ten percent of volume. Revenue falls to ninety four and a half. [[note]]Pricing power comes mostly from industry structure and competitive strategy: brand, differentiation, and few close substitutes.
beats.dol: Costs behave differently. Fixed costs stay put as sales change. Variable costs move with sales. [[setup]]Say sales are one thousand, variable costs are forty percent, and fixed costs are four hundred. Operating profit is two hundred. [[up]]Sales rise ten percent, to eleven hundred. Variable costs rise to four forty, fixed costs stay at four hundred, and operating profit is two sixty. [[dol]]Operating profit rose thirty percent. The degree of operating leverage is the ratio of the two changes: three. [[note]]The higher the share of fixed costs, the higher the operating leverage, and the more profit swings with sales.
beats.dfl: Financing adds a second layer. [[setup]]Interest of one hundred is a fixed cost. Operating profit of two hundred leaves pre-tax profit of one hundred. [[up]]Operating profit rises to two sixty. Interest stays at one hundred, so pre-tax profit becomes one sixty. [[dfl]]A thirty percent rise in operating profit became a sixty percent rise in pre-tax profit. The degree of financial leverage is two. [[total]]Together, a ten percent rise in sales becomes a sixty percent rise in net income. Total leverage is three times two, which is six. It cuts both ways.
beats.workingcap: Working capital shows how efficiently a company runs day to day. [[days]]Say inventory sits for thirty days, customers pay in two days, and suppliers are paid after twenty eight days. [[ccc]]The cash conversion cycle is thirty plus two, minus twenty eight: four days. [[note]]A cycle this short means the business needs very little working capital, because customers pay almost at once, and suppliers fund most of the inventory. Compare it with peers, and watch the trend.
beats.capital: Next, capital. Where did the money come from, and where did it go? [[src]]Sources: cash from operations, new borrowing, and new equity. [[use]]Uses: capital spending, acquisitions, dividends, buybacks, and building up cash. Both sides add to one thousand. [[tell]]Read the pattern. A company that funds growth from operations is healthier than one that borrows to pay dividends. [[nd]]Then test the capital structure. Net debt of six hundred over EBITDA of three hundred is two times. Compare with peers and with the trend. A company with high operating leverage should usually avoid high financial leverage.
beats.wrap: Four things to keep. [[w1]]A research report moves from business model, through financials and forecasts, to valuation and risks. [[w2]]Analyze revenue bottom-up and top-down, and judge pricing power. [[w3]]Operating leverage comes from fixed costs, and financial leverage from debt. Together they multiply the swing in profit. [[w4]]Check working capital, sources and uses of capital, and net debt over EBITDA.
